summary: Extends the RSVP ASSOCIATION object, which in GMPLS associates recovery LSPs with the LSPs they protect. It defines how the object can be used more broadly to associate RSVP state. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A name tag can link a spare road to the road it replaces. This memo lets the tag link other related things too.

questions: what is the rsvp association object
what is the extended association object
subtitle: Widening the RSVP ASSOCIATION object beyond GMPLS recovery, with larger identifiers for MPLS-TP.

tldr.problem: The RSVP ASSOCIATION object was defined only for tying GMPLS recovery LSPs together, yet other uses such as sharing resources across separate reservations need it, and its 16-bit ID is too small for some cases including MPLS-TP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC generalizes the Association ID, sets common matching rules for Path and Resv messages (identical objects mean an association), and defines IPv4 and IPv6 Extended ASSOCIATION objects with a Global Association Source and a variable Extended Association ID.
tldr.outcome: The object can associate state in any RSVP session type, not just GMPLS LSPs. The RFC updates RFC 2205, RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, and generalizes the field defined in RFC 4872.

today: RFC 6780 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2205, RFC 3209, RFC 3473 and RFC 4872.

sections.title: From Recovery to General Association
sections.content:
The RSVP ASSOCIATION object was defined for GMPLS-controlled Label Switched Paths (LSPs): in RFC 4872 and RFC 4873 it links recovery LSPs to the LSP they protect. This document expands its use to non-GMPLS and non-recovery contexts. The expanded use applies equally to GMPLS LSPs (RFC 3473), MPLS LSPs (RFC 3209) and plain RSVP sessions (RFC 2205).

The RFC gives three examples where separate reservations should share resources. In voice call-waiting, putting an A-B call on hold to take an A-C call should not double-count bandwidth. In a voice shared line, one number rings several endpoints, and separate unicast reservations would over-count bandwidth on shared links. With a symmetric NAT, flows to the same destination can show different destination ports outside the NAT, so ordinary RSVP sharing fails.

It also defines Extended ASSOCIATION objects usable with the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP), though their scope is not limited to MPLS-TP.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag used to say 'this spare goes with that road'. Now it can also say 'these two phone calls can share the same bandwidth', like two kids sharing one seat.

sections.title: A Wider Association ID
sections.content:
RFC 4872 defined the Association ID as a value assigned by the LSP head-end. Because other nodes may now originate associations, this RFC redefines it as a value assigned by the node that originated the association. Combined with the other fields in the object, it uniquely identifies an association.

The change does not affect the procedures of RFC 4872 or RFC 4873 or existing implementations. Association is found by exact ASSOCIATION object matching, and other matching mechanisms from RFC 4872, such as matching on Session IDs, are not generalized.
sections.plainLanguage: The label number now comes from whoever started the grouping, not only from the first router on a path.

sections.title: Path and Resv Association Rules
sections.content:
Association is always found by matching Path state to Path state, or Resv state to Resv state, never Path to Resv. An upstream-initiated association is carried in Path messages. A downstream-initiated one is carried in Resv messages. The sending node decides when to include the object, and to link several sessions it MUST include an identical ASSOCIATION object in the messages of each one, since this RFC defines no type-specific rules.

The originator MUST format the object as in Section 16.1 of RFC 4872, set the Association Type for the kind of association, set the Association ID to a value unique within the Association Source, and set the Association Source to a unique address of the originating node.

A receiving node MUST check each ASSOCIATION object for a type it supports, then compare it with the objects held in the state of all other sessions. An association exists when all fields are the same. Matching MUST continue after a first match, because more than one association may exist. Unless type-specific rules say otherwise, nodes MUST forward received ASSOCIATION objects unmodified, including those with unknown types.
sections.plainLanguage: If two reservations carry exactly the same tag, the routers know they belong together. Routers that do not understand the tag still pass it along untouched.

sections.title: Association Types
sections.content:
Two association types are defined: recovery and resource sharing. Recovery applies only in the recovery context of RFC 4872 and RFC 4873. Resource sharing, with Association Type value 2 as in RFC 4873, is applicable to any context and any RSVP session type, in both Path and Resv messages. Implementations compliant with this document MUST support it.

Once such an association is identified, the admission-control function MUST treat resources as shared across the associated sessions. How sharing is reflected depends on the implementation, since admission control is outside the scope of RSVP. A node that sees an unknown association type simply forwards the objects, and MAY also record the association, for example to expose it through a management interface.
sections.plainLanguage: One kind of tag means 'share the seat'. When a router sees it, it counts the shared seat only once.

sections.title: Extended ASSOCIATION Objects
sections.content:
The ASSOCIATION objects of RFC 4872 have a 16-bit Association ID, so a source can allocate up to 65536 associations and no more. That can be too few where a central entity manages many associations. MPLS-TP LSPs also need an operator-unique global identifier (RFC 6370) that includes the operator's Autonomous System Number. The new objects address both limits.

Both objects use Class-Num 199: the IPv4 Extended ASSOCIATION object has C-Type 3 and the IPv6 Extended ASSOCIATION object has C-Type 4. Beyond the RFC 4872 fields they add:

  • Global Association Source (4 bytes): a global identifier, or 0 for none. When non-zero, the Global_ID from RFC 6370 SHALL be used unless local policy overrides it. A zero SHOULD be limited to entities within one operator. If derived from a 2-octet ASN, the two high-order octets MUST be zero.
  • Extended Association ID (variable, 4-byte aligned): extra data scoped by the Association Source. It MAY be omitted, but MUST be included when the Association ID is not enough to identify the association uniquely.

With no Extended Association ID, the object Length MUST be 16 for IPv4 or 28 for IPv6. Otherwise Length covers the added bytes, including pad bytes. Processing is identical to the base objects: matching still compares all fields. Implementations SHOULD support the extended objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The old tag only had room for so many numbers. The new, longer tag adds a company code and optional extra writing, so there is room for far more.

sections.title: Compatibility with Older Nodes
sections.content:
The ASSOCIATION object class number has the form 11bbbbbb, so a node that does not support it ignores the object but forwards it unmodified, as RFC 2205 requires. Transit nodes that know ASSOCIATION but not the Extended C-Types will also pass any received object on unchanged.

An egress node that supports ASSOCIATION but not the extended C-Types may generate an Unknown object C-Type error, which propagates back to the ingress node for standard error handling. Operators who want a function tied to a particular association type should make sure every node expected to act on the association supports that type.
sections.plainLanguage: Older routers pass the new tag along without reading it. If the last router cannot read it at all, it sends back an error.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security considerations. Part of it reviews procedures already defined in RFC 4872 and RFC 4873. The broader use in Section 3 does not fundamentally expand the association function, and the extra 32 bits in the extended objects convey information not fundamentally different from what RSVP already carries.

For general MPLS and GMPLS security issues, including RSVP's chain of trust security model, it points to the framework in RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag does not let anyone do anything new, so it does not add new dangers.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
In the RSVP Parameters registry, IANA assigned two new C-Types under class 199 (ASSOCIATION): C-Type 3 for the IPv4 Extended Association and C-Type 4 for the IPv6 Extended Association.

In the GMPLS Association Type registry, IANA updated the Resource Sharing entry (value 2) to cite both RFC 4873 and this RFC, and corrected a duplicate use of the marker (R) by changing it to (S). There are no other IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers was updated with the two new tag types and a corrected note.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total object length in bytes; 16 when no Extended Association ID is present.

fields.name: Association Type
fields.desc: Kind of association, as in RFC 4872.

fields.name: Association ID
fields.desc: Value assigned by the originating node.

fields.name: IPv4 Association Source
fields.desc: Unique address of the originating node.

fields.name: Global Association Source
fields.desc: Global identifier, or zero if none.
